findings.claim: When asked which commandment was the greatest, he said that loving God with your whole heart is the first and greatest commandment, and that a second is like it: love your neighbour as yourself (Luke 10:25-37).
findings.truth: That wording is Matthew 22:37-39 (parallel Mark 12:28-31), where Jesus himself calls it 'the first and greatest commandment' and says 'the second is like it'. In Luke 10:25-28 it is the expert in the law who states the two commands and Jesus replies 'You have answered correctly'; Jesus never uses the 'first and greatest' formula there. Luke 10:29-37 then gives the Good Samaritan.
findings.evidence: NIV Matthew 22:37-39 vs Luke 10:25-28; scripture attribution check

findings.claim: Jesus taught his followers to ask God to forgive them "as we forgive those who sin against us" (Matthew 6:5-13).
findings.truth: Quoted text attributed to a Bible reference is not the Bible wording. NIV Matthew 6:12 reads 'And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.' 'Forgive us our sins as we forgive those who sin against us' is the modern liturgical version of the Lord's Prayer, not scripture.
findings.evidence: NIV Matthew 6:12; Church of England Common Worship text of the Lord's Prayer

findings.claim: Christian charities such as the Salvation Army and Shelter carry the church's commitment to social justice beyond its walls.
findings.truth: Shelter is a secular, non-denominational housing and homelessness charity (registered 1966). Its founders included clergy, but it has no Christian affiliation and is not a Christian charity. Tearfund is the Christian relief and development agency the spec itself names ('The work of Tearfund: Christian beliefs in action').
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Shelter (charity)' - registered charity, no denominational designation, secular operations; spec p.36 worldwide Church

findings.claim: Roman Catholicism is the largest single denomination globally and in the UK.
findings.truth: True globally, wrong for the UK. Anglicanism is the largest UK denomination by affiliation - about 23.9 million baptised Anglicans, and 53% of UK Christians in the 2021-22 census identified as Anglican, with Catholicism second.

findings.claim: Do not just state the teaching - examiners reward you for explaining how it influences behaviour.
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. Nothing in the spec says what examiners reward. State the mark consequence directly instead.
findings.evidence: spec 3 (assessment objectives) carries no such statement

findings.claim: The 15-mark evaluation questions in lessons 2, 3 and 4 carry a four-bullet instruction: 'In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching / give reasoned arguments to support this statement / give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view / reach a justified conclusion.'
findings.truth: That bullet rubric is another board's 12-mark evaluation wording, pasted onto a 15-mark question. This paper's 15-mark question asks the candidate to evaluate the statement showing that more than one point of view has been considered. Lesson 1's 15-mark question already uses the correct house form, so the unit is also internally inconsistent. Copyright rule also bars pasting a board's rubric wording.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Component 2 assessment description (1 hour, 25%, 60 marks + 6 SPaG, compulsory questions); lesson 1 practice question 6 for the correct form

findings.claim: Pilgrimage sites taught are the Holy Land, Lourdes, Holywell and the Marian Shrine of Cardigan.
findings.truth: The spec names exactly two pilgrimage sites - Walsingham and Taize - and neither appears anywhere in the unit. Lourdes is another board's named site. The four sites taught are all factually correct, so the fix adds the two required sites rather than removing the others.
findings.evidence: spec p.36, Practices: 'The importance of pilgrimage: Walsingham, Taize'; Wikipedia 'Walsingham' (Norfolk; Richeldis de Faverches, 1061; Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox shrines) and 'Taize Community' (Saone-et-Loire, Burgundy; Brother Roger, 1940; ecumenical; over 100,000 young people a year)

findings.claim: Roman Catholics recognise seven sacraments; most Protestant churches focus on two: baptism and the Eucharist. All agree that these rites were instituted by Jesus himself.
findings.truth: 'All agree' is wrong. Quakers (the Society of Friends) and the Salvation Army use no sacraments at all. The spec requires 'Diverse beliefs regarding Sacraments' and names the Society of Friends, so this omission is also a scope gap.
findings.evidence: spec p.36, Practices: 'Diverse beliefs regarding Sacraments' and 'with reference to Society of Friends and Evangelical worship'

findings.claim: scripture defined as 'A collection of 66 books (39 Old Testament, 27 New Testament)' in the content definition and in the glossary.
findings.truth: 66 is the Protestant canon. Catholic Bibles contain 73 books (46 Old Testament including the deuterocanonical books, plus 27 New Testament); Orthodox canons are larger again. A unit that teaches Catholic and Protestant divergence throughout should not state one tradition's canon as the Bible.
findings.evidence: Protestant vs Catholic canon; the lesson itself contrasts Catholic and Protestant belief on sacraments and the Eucharist

findings.claim: Match each person of the Trinity to the biblical passage most associated with them in the spec.
findings.truth: None of the three passages used (Luke 15:11-32, John 1:1-3 and 1:14, Galatians 5:22-23) is a spec-named passage. The spec names John 10:30 and John 14:6-11 for the Trinity, John 1:1-5 for the Word and Spirit in creation, and Acts 2:1-6 for the Spirit. Telling a student these are the spec's passages is false; the passages themselves are correctly matched.
findings.evidence: spec pp.34-35, Beliefs and teachings: the nature of God, the Trinity, creation, salvation

findings.claim: The unit's scripture references are largely not the ones the spec sets: crucifixion taught from Mark 15:1-39 (spec: Matthew 27:28-50), resurrection from John 20:1-21 (spec: Luke 24:1-9, 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, 12-14), ascension from Acts 1:9-11 (spec: Luke 24:50-53), Messiah from Matthew 16:13-17 (not in the spec). The nature of God and the Trinity in lesson 1 use none of Exodus 7-11, Exodus 14:21, Psalm 86:15, John 3:16, Romans 8:37-39, Job 1:8-12 and 42:1-6, John 10:30 or John 14:6-11.
findings.truth: Nothing taught is factually wrong - every passage cited is genuine and correctly quoted - but a student finishes the unit having met almost none of the passages the paper is built around, and the spec says 'References to relevant sources of wisdom and authority are expected'. Options: (a) leave it, since any relevant source is creditable; (b) a follow-up pass adding the spec passages alongside the existing ones, which is additive and needs no re-narration of corrections; (c) rebuild the scripture spine on the spec list. Recommend (b).
findings.evidence: spec pp.34-35, Component 2 Route A specific content column
findings.ruling: Leave: coverage/scope gap recorded as a follow-up build item (not a surgical fix).

findings.claim: Lesson 3 teaches divine command ethics, situational ethics, agape and Joseph Fletcher as part of the Christianity unit; several Component 2 areas are absent from the unit entirely.
findings.truth: Absolute and relative morality, conscience and Christian teachings on forgiveness (Matthew 18:21-22, Matthew 6) sit in Route A Component 1, Theme 3 (Issues of Good and Evil), not in the Christianity component. They are still examinable on this route, so nothing is wasted. Meanwhile the Christianity component's own content is missing: Christianity in Britain (2011 vs 2021 census figures), the worldwide Church (Tearfund, persecution of Christians, mission, the Ecumenical Movement - only the World Council of Churches gets a mention), how Christians celebrate Christmas and Easter, and the liturgical / informal / individual worship contrast with the Society of Friends and Evangelical worship. 'Evangelism' is one of the eight named concepts and never appears in any lesson. Recommend adding a fifth lesson covering Christianity in Britain, the worldwide Church, festivals and worship styles, and keeping the lesson 3 ethics material as themes-paper revision rather than cutting it.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1 Component 1 Theme 3 (lines 1521-1585) vs 2.2 Component 2 (pp.34-36) including the eight named concepts
findings.ruling: Leave: coverage/scope gap recorded as a follow-up build item (not a surgical fix).

findings.claim: Question 1's mark scheme reads '... Incarnation is described in John 1:14. StudyVault rubric: Mastering - two precise beliefs ...'
findings.truth: An internal authoring label has leaked into a student-facing mark scheme. Not a factual error, so no edit, but worth a sweep across other units built from the same template.

findings.claim: The resurrection paragraph cites John 20:1-21 but quotes 'Receive the Holy Spirit'.
findings.truth: That line is John 20:22, just outside the cited range. The rest of the paragraph (empty tomb, gardener, wounds shown) is inside 20:1-21 and correct.

findings.claim: Genesis 1:1-3 describes God bringing the universe into existence through his spoken word: light, sky, land, and life all come from his creative command.
findings.truth: Only light is created in Genesis 1:1-3. Sky, land and life come in Genesis 1:6-25. The spec sets 'Genesis 1-3' for creation, so the wider reference would be safe.
findings.evidence: NIV Genesis 1:1-3 vs 1:6-25; spec p.34 'Creation: Genesis 1-3'

findings.claim: The 8-mark questions in lessons 2, 3 and 4 append 'Refer to a source of Christian teaching in your answer.' / 'Refer to sources of Christian teaching in your answer.', and the question type labels read 'Explain Two Beliefs'.
findings.truth: That instruction line and the 'explain two beliefs' stem are another board's shape. The marks themselves (2 / 5 / 8 / 15) are correct for this paper and the advice is sound for any board, so this is not worth an edit on its own. Fold it into any future rebuild of the practice set.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Component 2 assessment description; question-form comparison

findings.claim: For the 15-mark evaluation question, avoid writing in bullet points - this limits you to description and blocks evaluation marks.
findings.truth: Overstated. Bullet points do not formally block evaluation marks. The true reason continuous prose matters is that spelling, punctuation and grammar are assessed on the extended-writing questions on this paper (12 SPaG marks across the qualification, 6 on this component).

summary: Four lessons, seventeen findings (10 FIX, 2 ADJUDICATE, 5 NOTE), fourteen edits across all four lessons - no lesson came through clean. The mark-affecting errors are all in lessons 3 and 4: the 'first and greatest commandment' wording attributed to Luke 10 instead of Matthew 22, the Lord's Prayer quoted in its liturgical rather than its biblical wording, Shelter presented as a Christian charity when it is secular, Roman Catholicism called the largest UK denomination when Anglicanism is, 'all agree' on sacraments when Quakers and the Salvation Army use none, and the Protestant 66-book canon stated as the Bible. Two exam-form fixes: a fabricated 'examiners reward' claim, and another board's four-bullet evaluation rubric on the 15-mark questions in three lessons. Two scope items are left for adjudication - the unit's scripture spine barely touches the passages the spec sets, and whole Component 2 areas (Christianity in Britain, the worldwide Church, festivals, worship styles, the concept of evangelism) are missing while lesson 3 teaches themes-paper ethics.
